title: What exactly is in the deal between the UK and the EU?
text: The British prime minister, Andy Burnham, the European Council president, Antonio Costa, and the president of the European Commission, Ursula von der Leyen announced an agreement on Friday. Photograph: Yves Herman/Reuters View image in fullscreen The British prime minister, Andy Burnham, the European Council president, Antonio Costa, and the president of the European Commission, Ursula von der Leyen announced an agreement on Friday. Photograph: Yves Herman/Reuters Explainer What exactly is in the deal between the UK and the EU? The two sides have come to agreements on food and drink, emissions trading and the youth exchange scheme Burnham has agreed EU reset deal with tuition fees issue unresolved, says No 10 After months of on-off negotiations, leaks and late nights, the EU and UK have agreed a 12-page statement setting out the next steps in their relationship. What exactly have they agreed? The three deals The two sides have struck three deals long expected from this summit: food and drink, emissions trading and a youth exchange programme. The food and drink deal will ease Brexit controls on the vast majority of animal and plant products being traded between Britain and the EU, a boon for producers of meat, dairy, and flowers among many other products. If all goes well – and there is still an if – the deal will apply from 1 March 2028. The energy deal relinks the British and EU emissions trading schemes, shielding industrial producers on both sides from levies on polluting products, such as steel and fertilisers, as well as electricity. This should enter into force in 2028. Under the youth experience scheme, up to 100,000 British people each year would be able to live, work, travel and study in the EU for up to three years. The same number of young Europeans would be able to come to the UK. Young people should be able to take advantage of the scheme by 2030 at the latest. The president of the European Commission, Ursula von der Leyen, who studied at the London School of Economics when she was young, said it was a “very emotional moment” to strike the youth mobility agreement, while Andy Burnham addressed young people – saying: “This deal really is about lifting your life chances.” What about tuition fees? The two sides agreed to kick the can down the road for six months. The EU wants to ensure that young Europeans pay the domestic rate of tuition to study at British universities, capped at £9,790 in the current academic year, rather than the international rate, which can be four or five times higher. Under pressure from cash-strapped universities, the government has resisted this claim. The EU agreed a statement on Friday – not part of the joint text – that said it would not sign off the three deals (food and drink, emissions trading youth mobility), without a deal on equal treatment on tuition fees. The prime minister rejected this link, saying the deal was done. EU leaders have also expressed confidence in resolving the issue within six months. A seat at the table As a condition of getting the food and drink and emissions trading deals, the UK will be required to align with EU law in these areas, including new rules that it never had a say in writing. The UK will be allowed to attend relevant EU meetings as an observer without voting rights. After lobbying from Britain’s EU allies in northern Europe, Britain got a small upgrade to be in the room to observe discussions on future laws when they relate to “emergencies of specific relevance” to the UK, such as animal disease outbreaks. But it still cannot vote. The details are outlined in a separate text not in the main agreement. Energy The next major agreement is bringing the UK back into the EU’s internal electricity market. The two sides aimed to wrap up this deal in 2027. This is a priority for five EU member states: Germany, Belgium, the Netherlands, Denmark and Luxembourg. They argue that Britain’s inclusion in the EU electricity market is essential to take advantage of the nascent green power boom in the North Sea. In return for market access, the UK will be required to contribute to the EU budget to aid the development of poorer EU regions. But there are no details on the size of the UK contribution. View image in fullscreen A windfarm in the North Sea off Skegness, Lincolnshire. Photograph: Andrew Aitchison/In Pictures/Getty Images Migration The UK agreed to work closely with the EU’s “Channel action plan”, which aims to crack down on smugglers who organise small boat crossings. The agreement will see law enforcement intelligence sharing between the UK and the EU, working closer with agencies such as Europol and the European border agency Frontex, and improved maritime surveillance from French authorities. The agreement promises “a new structured dialogue” on migration, with both sides pledging to disrupt smuggling networks, strengthening border management in the Channel to stop small boat crossings, and work more closely with countries along migration routes. Both sides will require “shared financial commitments” given the “shared nature” of the challenges, according to the agreement. Von der Leyen said Britain and the bloc would work together along the entire migration route and to prevent dangerous Channel crossings, which she argued would also save lives. Burnham also expressed interest in the plans of five EU member states to negotiate an offshore “returns hub” with Rwanda for people with no right to stay in the EU. Touring artists In a significant win for the UK, the EU has agreed to “explore further mutually beneficial solutions” on touring artists. This does not sound like much. But the Labour government has spent more than two years making the case for easier access to the EU for travelling artists, musicians and performers, who face cumbersome work permits and complex rules for tour vehicles and equipment. Government-commissioned research suggests Brexit touring barriers have cost the UK sector £208m and nearly 2,500 jobs. The EU has long refused to open discussions, so an agreement to talk is a breakthrough. Nonetheless it might not seem much to artists snared in red tape when working on the continent. The Musicians Union general secretary, Naomi Pohl, said members would be “extremely disappointed”, adding that she hoped “resolving this issue will be a priority”. Tech The document details plans to launch a new bilateral agreement – the EU-UK digital partnership – early next year. It will aim to increase cooperation on technology issues such as AI, connectivity, critical technologies, digital wallets and online safety with both parties maintaining “regulatory autonomy”. Mutual recognition of qualifications In a potential advance for the UK, the EU appears ready to expand talks on the mutual recognition of professional qualifications, beyond existing negotiations on architects. The statement welcomes “significant progress” on mutual recognition of professional qualifications for architects under the trade and cooperation agreement (TCA), and both sides agreed to “explore” arrangements in other professions.
